name: read
description: map files with outline; read only the lines you need
body:
READ — reading files without wasting tokens

Use:      minas read <path> [--lines <start>:<end>]   (any file, buffer-free — ADR-0048)
          minas get --lines <start>:<end>            (current buffer only)
Output:   numbered lines: {"n":1500,"text":"..."}  (1-origin, end may be empty = last line)

Rules
- Read only the lines you need (measured: ranged read cuts task tokens by ~51% vs
  whole-file reads).
- `minas read <path>` reads ANY file without touching the current buffer — no
  Open/apply needed just to look (a plain `minas read <path>` prints the raw
  text; `--lines` prints numbered lines). `minas get` reads only the buffer
  (last Open/apply) and returns the full snapshot; add `--brief` to drop the
  history fields (events/activity) when you only need text/checksum/dirty
  (rust2 #21: 78-char buffer 79KB -> ~830B). Same `--brief` works on `wait`
  and `edit` responses.
- On an unfamiliar file, minas outline FIRST (structure + exact spans for a
  fraction of the bytes), then read only the symbol you need; minas at
  <path> <line>:<col> names the symbol enclosing a spot you are about to touch,
  so both reads and edits happen at symbol granularity.
- For types, minas hover <path> <line>:<col> returns the signature without
  any read; to find where a name lives in the workspace, minas symbol
  <path> <query> replaces rg (both ADR-0032).
- The numbered output lets you paste the exact text you saw into `minas apply`
  as the <old> argument — read and edit share one contract.
- Out-of-range start returns an explained zero result, e.g.
  "no lines in 3000..3100: file has 2000 lines" — this is not an error, just pick
  a valid range.
- A whole-file read is allowed only when you really need the full text; prefer
  --lines otherwise. A whole-file `minas get` is allowed only when you need the
  checksum or diagnostic machinery of the snapshot.

name: wait
description: minas wait <generation>: block until the state moves (settled), then return the snapshot
body:
WAIT — block until the document moves, without polling

Use:      minas wait <generation>            (blocking; returns the snapshot)
          minas wait --brief <generation>    (same, minus events/activity — ~1KB)

Rules
- Pass a generation you already saw (e.g. from `minas apply`'s result or
  `minas get --brief`). It blocks until the daemon's generation exceeds it,
  then returns that snapshot. No polling, no idle traffic (ADR-0014).
- Content changes are SETTLED before the wait returns (rust2 #16/#18): an edit
  batch (apply = Open -> replace_range -> Save) wakes you only after the text
  stops changing (~120ms quiet), so you get the settled text, not the pre-edit
  text at the Open stage. Several hunks (or several quick edits) are swallowed
  into one wake with the final state.
- Already-quiet returns immediately: if the last content change is older than
  the quiet window, `wait <old-generation>` answers in ~10ms — usable as a
  cheap "has anything moved?" check.
- If no content change ever arrives it falls back after ~500ms and returns the
  current snapshot (ADR-0014's immediate-return contract is preserved); the CLI
  bounds the whole wait at 90s and exits 2 (retryable) on timeout.
- Open/Save/mode changes alone do not wake it — only content-changing events
  (edit, Undo/Redo, external change, rename). If you need to observe a focus
  change, use `get` instead.
- In a wait loop, always use --brief: the full snapshot per wake is ~68KB
  (rust2 #15).

name: edit
description: edit via content (minas apply); never compute positions
body:
EDIT — content-resolved edits (the front door)

Use:      minas apply <path> <old> <new>
          minas apply <path> --pair old.txt new.txt [--pair old2.txt new2.txt ...]
                                            (recommended for batches: same atomic
                                             contract as --hunks-stdin, but texts
                                             come from files — no JSON escaping)
          minas apply <path> --hunks-stdin   (JSON array of {"old","new"} for many edits)
What it does: Open -> find <old> -> verify (checksum + expected_text) -> replace -> Save,
all in one command. Position math is done for you.

Rules
- Positions in minas are CHAR offsets (never bytes / UTF-16). Do not derive
  them from byte lengths — a Japanese comment or emoji shifts everything
  (rust2 #17). This is another reason to let apply resolve old->new.
- Prefer content-resolved edits over positional ones. Measured: positional editing
  (`minas edit` with computed char offsets) fails 0/5 vs 3/5 for content-resolved,
  costs ~5x tokens, and can silently apply to the WRONG occurrence (a successful
  exit with the wrong spot changed). Do not compute start/end char indices.
- `minas edit` now REQUIRES expected_text: a positional edit without it can
  silently corrupt (whole-document checksum cannot detect a shifted range;
  rust2 #5-2). Give the current text at start..end, or use apply.
- After an edit, DETECT errors with `minas check <path>` (ADR-0032): it waits
  for LSP diagnostics and returns only errors — no full text, no parsing. Exit 2
  means at least one error diagnostic (warnings alone exit 0); exit 0 is NOT a
  verified clean (an empty check is always settled:false). A green verdict
  requires the real build (cargo check / cargo test).
- Locate before you edit: minas outline / minas at return the exact span of
  the symbol you are changing, so your <old> text targets the right region
  instead of a look-alike occurrence elsewhere.
- One invocation replaces the FIRST occurrence of <old>. Repeat for the next one,
  or batch many changes with --pair / --hunks-stdin (faster: ~3x on one connection).
- Atomicity covers the buffer too, not just disk: before any edit is sent, all
  old texts are verified in sequence; if one is missing the whole batch aborts
  with nothing applied, and a later `read` returns the disk truth (rust2: no
  phantom partial-apply). A repeated identical (old,new) pair hits occurrences
  in order — N copies of the same hunk replace occurrences 1..N (rust2 #4-2).
- --hunks-stdin reports the per-hunk outcome: the JSON has "edits" (accepted)
  and "edits_noop", and hunk-level stderr lines distinguish two no-op kinds
  (rust2 #10):
    `HUNK SKIPPED: #N (old == new)` — you sent an identity hunk (same old and
      new); it is your input mistake, nothing was applied.
    `HUNK NO-OP: #N (changed nothing)` — the replacement left the text as-is
      (defensive; an identity hunk is caught before sending).
  Batching must not hide a silently-unapplied hunk — check "edits_noop" when
  the diff you expected did not appear.
- --pair is the file-based form of --hunks-stdin: each `--pair old.txt new.txt`
  becomes one hunk, all applied on one connection and saved once (same atomic
  contract — an undetected old aborts everything, disk untouched). Use it when
  your old/new texts contain `\n` or quotes and hand-escaping JSON is friction.
- Small targeted replacements beat one huge <old> block: a big mismatch wipes too
  much. For whole-file rewrites use --whole-stdin.
- When machine-generating a hunk that PREPENDS to a multi-line <old>, the <new>
  must be "the prepended text + the ENTIRE old text, once". Writing the doc line
  and then repeating old's first line duplicates it (e.g. two `pub id: TodoId,`
  fields -> E0124; rust2 #19). Prepend means insert before, not around.
- A non-existent <path> is created as an empty file first (so Save can create
  it); missing parent directories are created too (`apply src/domain/mod.rs
  --whole-stdin` works even when src/domain/ does not exist yet).
  A content-resolved edit needs <old> to already exist, so `apply <path>
  <old> <new>` on a new file always ends in NOT FOUND — create content with
  `apply <path> --whole-stdin` (or --whole). On failure the empty file is
  removed again.
- An empty whole-file replacement against a non-empty file is REFUSED unless
  --allow-empty (subprocess stdin not connected is the usual cause; rust2
  #5-1). To create a genuinely empty file, `touch` it or use --allow-empty.
- On rejection (exit 2) the message names the expected/found text and the range.
  Re-read that spot fresh, fix, retry — do not blind-retry.

name: outline
description: minas outline <path>: symbol tree (name/kind/span) without full text
body:
OUTLINE — map a file's structure without reading it

Use:      minas outline <path>
          minas outline <path> --recursive [--depth N]  (cross files — ADR-0049)
Output:   compact JSON tree, no file text: each symbol is
          {"name", "kind", "range", "selection_range", "children"},
          kinds: Module/Function/Method/Type/Enum/Constant/Variable/Other

Rules
- On an unfamiliar file, outline FIRST: every symbol's name, kind, and exact
  span for a fraction of a read. Measured (7,981-line file): outline + at =
  55 KB vs a full minas get = 814 KB (~93% fewer bytes).
- --recursive follows file-scoped modules (`mod name;` → the file that defines
  them) and inlines their symbols as children — one call maps a whole crate
  instead of one outline per file. Default depth 3; --depth N implies --recursive
  and sets the cap (--depth 1 = direct child modules only). A "truncated" note on
  stderr means the 500-symbol cap cut the tree (still exit 0; per-file outline
  for the parts you need).
- range and selection_range are objects {"anchor","head"} holding char offsets
  (the same unit as DocumentEdit positions); selection_range is only the name
  token. Use them to choose WHICH lines to read (minas get --lines /
  minas read --lines) and WHICH text to target in minas apply — read at symbol
  granularity, not file granularity.
- The tree is nested and grep-able: find the function you need by name instead
  of scanning text.
- The first outline on a path is cold (seconds: project load + LSP settle);
  the daemon caches it, so pull it once at session start and reuse the ranges
  for reads / at / edits. Warm calls are ~0.1s.
- Exit 1 = not supported (no LSP server for this language) or bad input;
  exit 2 = retryable LSP error (retry once later, then give up).

name: at
description: minas at <path> <line>:<col>: enclosing symbol + its exact range
body:
AT — the symbol enclosing a position, with its exact range

Use:      minas at <path> <line>:<col>   (1-origin, like get --lines)

Units: all positions minas exposes are CHAR offsets (not bytes, not UTF-16).
Never compute offsets from byte length — a Japanese comment or an emoji
(1 char / 4 bytes) shifts them immediately. Better still: let apply resolve
the old text and never compute a position yourself (rust2 #17).
Range vs selection_range: `range` is the whole item INCLUDING attributes
(e.g. a `#[allow(...)]` above an fn), `selection_range` is the name token.
Use `range` for --lines / apply and expect it to start before the attribute
block (rust2 #17).
Output:   pretty JSON, no file text: {"name", "kind", "range",
          "selection_range", "found"}. found=false is a SUCCESS (exit 0):
          the position is in no symbol — pick a different spot.

Rules
- Before touching a spot, ask what it belongs to: at names the enclosing
  function/type and its exact span, so your read and your <old> text are
  scoped to the right region — no full-file reads, no guessing which function
  a matching string lives in.
- selection_range is the substring of the symbol NAME: the address for
  rename-style edits and for locating the token named in a rejection message.
- Ranges are {"anchor","head"} objects of char offsets: pair the span with
  minas get --lines to see the actual lines before editing inside it.
- Warm after an outline of that path: ~0.1s (measured 6.5s -> 0.09s cold to
  cached); the cold cost is paid by the one session-start outline, not by
  every at.
- Exit 1/2 as with outline/rename (1 = not supported / bad input, 2 =
  retryable LSP error).

name: rename
description: minas rename <path> <old> <new> (semantic); apply for a few
body:
RENAME — semantic rename vs apply (measured decision)

minas has a built-in semantic rename (content-addressed, ADR-0029):
    minas rename <path> <old> <new>
- Use it for renames with MANY occurrences or MULTIPLE files. Measured (3 files,
  21 occurrences): LSP rename 5/5 success vs apply loop 2/5 (apply kept missing
  occurrences), ~half the tokens (-49%) and cost (-57%).
- It renames the definition and ALL references (imports, calls) in one call,
  saves to disk, and prints the impact: `renamed: old -> new (N files, M edits)`
  plus a `changed:` list — verify the impact is what you meant.
- Exit 1 = not supported / bad input (do not retry), exit 2 = retryable
  (symbol not found, LSP error, stale analysis — re-read and retry).

If only content-editing is available (minas apply):
- For a handful of occurrences in ONE file, loop with apply. Measured on a small
  file it is as cheap as LSP rename.
- For many occurrences or cross-file renames you MUST verify with a final
  `minas references <path> <old>` (or grep/read) that no old name remains —
  measured failure mode is silently leaving one occurrence behind.

Never try to re-implement the rename by hand-editing each call site when an LSP
rename tool exists.

name: references
description: minas references <path> <old>: list a symbol's references
body:
REFERENCES — impact check before/after a rename (ADR-0029)

    minas references <path> <old>

- Resolves <old> like rename (first identifier occurrence) and lists every
  reference with the definition: `path:line` (1-origin), e.g.
- Resolution rule: <old> is matched as an identifier and resolved to the FIRST
  such occurrence in <path> (comments/strings excluded). With several
  same-named fields in one file, point <path> at the definition's file so the
  first occurrence there is the one you mean — the daemon does not guess which
  of several identical names you wanted.
      2 references in 1 files:
      /abs/path.rs:4
      /abs/path.rs:1
- Use before a rename to see what will change, or after apply-based edits to
  verify nothing was missed — the T5 failure mode is a silently-left occurrence.
- The output is locations only (token-cheap): read a location with
  `minas get --lines <line>:<line>`.
- Exit 1/2 as with rename.

name: check
description: minas check <path>...: wait for diagnostics, returns only errors
body:
CHECK — find errors fast; it never certifies clean (ADR-0032)

Use:      minas check <path> [<path> ...]
          minas check --crate-root src/lib.rs [--include-tests]
                                    (expand to every .rs under src/ [+ tests/]
                                     and check them all in one call — the
                                     edit→verify loop for multi-file breakage)
Output:   compact JSON, no file text: an array with one entry per path:
          {"path", "total", "diagnostics", "settled", "verdict"}, where each
          diagnostic is {"severity", "line" (1-origin), "col" (1-origin, char
          units), "start", "end", "message"}. A path whose pull FAILED still
          gets an entry, carrying "error" (total 0, settled false, verdict
          "failed") — so an empty array never means "all paths failed"
          (ADR-0046). verdict is `errors (n)` / `warnings (n)` / `hints (n)` /
          `clean-unverified` / `unlinked-unverified` / `failed`, counted by
          diagnostic severity — branch on it directly (ADR-0045/0052).
          `unlinked-unverified` means the path is not inside any project (no
          ancestor Cargo.toml / package.json / pyproject.toml / go.mod / .git):
          the LSP has nothing to analyze, so even a file with syntax errors
          returns total 0 — never read it as clean (rust2 #21). Hints/Info
          (RA-only: inactive #[cfg] branches etc.) are never counted as
          warnings: check reports LSP diagnostics, not rustc lints, so
          "warnings (1)" here means an actual Warning diagnostic, not an
          unused-import lint (rust2 #9).
          `--summary` prints one `path: verdict` line per path instead of the
          JSON array (exit codes unchanged).
Exit:     0 = no error diagnostic was found — NOT a verified clean (see below),
          2 = at least one error diagnostic, or a retryable LSP failure,
          1 = not supported / bad input.

Rules
- check FINDS errors; it cannot PROVE the code is clean. Exit 2 is
  authoritative (a real error); exit 0 is not green. A green verdict requires
  the real build (cargo check / cargo test).
- After an edit (minas apply / edit), run check INSTEAD of wait + get +
  JSON-parsing the snapshot: it waits for LSP diagnostics to settle and returns
  only the diagnostics — the wait, the full text and the parsing are gone. It
  replaces the snapshot round trip, NOT the build.
- Pass multiple paths to verify every file you touched in one call
  (ADR-0046): `minas check src/lib.rs src/other.rs`. When a cross-cutting
  change (new field, new enum variant) breaks several files at once and you
  cannot enumerate them, use --crate-root: it checks the whole crate tree
  (src/) plus tests/ with --include-tests in one round trip (rust2 #7).
- Read "error" on an entry before concluding anything from "total": it means
  the pull failed (not "no errors"), and the message names the reason (session
  lock busy = retry, server dead = the next .rs Open respawns it).
- The 1-origin line is the address for `minas get --lines <n>:<n>`; the
  char range locates the span whose text you paste as the <old> argument of
  `minas apply`. The line:col pair is the address for
  `minas at / peek / hover <path> <line>:<col>` — pass it straight through
  without computing anything (ADR-0047).
- It is an LSP fast path (incremental), not a compiler: for semantics beyond
  the LSP (borrow checker etc.) still run the real build.
- check reports only rust-analyzer's diagnostics. rustc lints that RA does not
  compute (unused imports, dead_code, unreachable_patterns, deprecated usage,
  ...) never appear — they are invisible to check's pull (verified 2026-09-12:
  unused import / unused variable / unreachable pattern / deprecated call /
  never-read field / unused arg all returned clean-unverified). Even a genuine
  `warnings (n)` verdict is rare in practice: RA's semantic pull is almost all
  Error + Hint (inactive #[cfg] code), and Warning requires the LSP server to
  actually emit one. Zero warnings is something only the real build (cargo
  check with warnings) can show; check is an ERROR-detection shortcut, never a
  warning detector.
- settled is not a clean/not-clean flag. An empty result is ALWAYS
  settled=false, even for a genuinely clean file — settled=true requires a
  non-empty set to repeat (ADR-0045/0052). Empty means "the pull reported
  nothing": it may be clean, or it may be an error the pull misses. It comes
  back fast (~0.6s) instead of burning a ~10s budget, and waiting would not
  turn it into a clean (ADR-0052). The verdict "clean-unverified" is the
  machine-readable spelling of that state — treat it as "run cargo", never as
  green.
- rust-analyzer's pull misses real errors (name typos, method resolution,
  cross-file type errors come back empty), so an empty result is never a reason
  to skip the build.

name: hover
description: minas hover <path> <line>:<col>: type & signature without full text
body:
HOVER — type/signature lookup without reading (ADR-0032)

Use:      minas hover <path> <line>:<col>   (1-origin, like get --lines)
Output:   compact JSON: {"path", "text"} — type + signature + doc, no file text.
          Empty text is a SUCCESS (exit 0): nothing to hover at that position
          (whitespace, comments).

Rules
- Before reading a definition to learn its type, hover the call site: the
  server returns the signature in one round trip (token-cheap).
- The doc comment is truncated (<=2000 chars) — the type/signature is the
  reliable part; read the doc only when the short part is not enough.
- Pair with minas peek <path> <line>:<col> to jump to the definition.
- Exit 1/2 as with outline/at (1 = not supported / bad input, 2 = retryable).

name: symbol
description: minas symbol <path> <query>: find where a name lives in the workspace
body:
SYMBOL — workspace search instead of rg (ADR-0032)

Use:      minas symbol <path> <query>
Output:   compact JSON array, no file text: each hit is
          {"name", "kind", "path", "line" (1-origin)} — read the location
          with `minas get --lines`.

Rules
- <path> is any file in the workspace (it anchors the workspace root);
  results can span the whole root, not just that file.
- Use it INSTEAD of rg when you need to know WHERE a name is defined or
  declared: the server returns exact symbols (no whole lines, no false
  positive comments/strings), and the hit range is the definition.
- Fuzzy matching varies by server; a broad query then narrowing by kind/line
  is cheaper than many greps.
- Exit 1 = not supported / bad input (empty query), 2 = retryable.

name: persist
description: minas edit leaves the buffer dirty; save explicitly
body:
PERSIST — when changes hit the disk

- `minas apply` (and --hunks-stdin) Save for you: after success the file on
  disk is updated.
- Raw `minas edit` does NOT save: the daemon buffer changes but the disk file
  stays old (dirty=true). If you used edit, persist with:
      minas exec "Save"
- When an edit succeeded but the buffer is dirty, minas prints a stderr note:
  "buffer is dirty (not saved); persist with: minas exec '"Save"'".
- Before relying on a file's on-disk content, prefer apply (which re-opens the
  file fresh) over mixing edit + assumptions.

name: errors
description: exit codes 0/1/2 and how to recover from rejections
body:
ERRORS — exit codes and recovery

Exit codes (applies to minas apply / edit / hunks):
  0  success (applied, or no-op)
  1  usage/CLI error — fix the arguments; do not retry the same call
  2  retryable failure — old text not found, checksum/expected_text mismatch,
     empty whole-file replacement refused (pass --allow-empty to truncate),
     or Save failed. Re-read the file fresh, then retry.

Blocking `minas wait <generation>` returns the full state snapshot when the
generation moves — use `minas wait --brief <generation>` to strip the history
fields (events/activity) from every wake; the wait loop pays this cost per
wake (rust2 #15: 68KB -> ~1KB). The daemon settles content changes before
returning (rust2 #16/#18): an edit batch (apply = Open -> replace_range ->
Save) wakes it only after the text stops changing (~120ms quiet), so the
returned text is the settled one, not the pre-edit text at the Open stage.
If the last content change is already older than the quiet window the wait
returns immediately (~10ms), so `wait <old generation>` stays a cheap check.
If no content change ever arrives it falls back after ~500ms (ADR-0014's
immediate-return contract is preserved).

Semantic commands (rename / references / outline / at / hover / symbol / check)
share 0/1/2 but classify differently: exit 1 = not supported / invalid input
(do not retry), exit 2 = retryable (symbol not found, LSP error — re-run once
later). Exceptions:
- minas at with no enclosing symbol is exit 0 (found=false), not an error —
  only the LSP request itself can fail.
- minas hover with nothing at the position is exit 0 (empty text), not an error.
- minas check returns exit 2 when at least one error diagnostic is present
  (warnings alone exit 0). So $?=1 = not supported / cannot open (do not
  retry), $?=2 = error found or a retryable LSP failure, $?=0 = no error found
  — and $?=0 is NOT a verified clean (an empty check is always settled:false):
  branch on $? for errors, but a green verdict requires the real build (cargo).
  Same classification as outline / at / rename (rust2 #23).

rename failure lines are prefixed `rename failed:` (success is
`renamed: old -> new (N files, M edits)`) so the two are never confused
(rust2 #23).

Rejections are the editor telling you what changed:
- "document changed since read"      -> the file moved; re-read and retry.
- "expected text mismatch: expected X,
  found Y at [lo,hi)" -> the range is not
  what you assumed; re-read THAT range (use --lines) and fix the old text.
- "NOT FOUND: text"                  -> the old string is not in the file; re-grep.

Recovery loop: read the reported spot with `minas get --lines`, correct the
old/new, retry. Never blind-retry a rejected edit.

External modification: the daemon auto-reloads files changed on disk (2s poll;
a reload detected by a command's Open path appears sooner). If the new size is
under half the old, the reload sets snapshot status "file shrank N -> M chars"
(rust2 #5-5/#6/#8) — it appears in the status field of the NEXT snapshot
(get / get --brief / apply response) and in the activity log. The status is a
GLOBAL one-shot (any document's snapshot may carry it), so it embeds the
affected path: "reloaded from disk (path: /abs/path.rs; ...)" — read the path
before acting. After any external tool touches a file you are editing, run
`minas get --brief` and read its status. The reload replaces the text AND its
undo history, so a truncated file cannot be undone; recover by re-applying
from a known-good source (git show > file, then apply). Note: the reload is watcher-
driven (2s poll), so the warning appears on the get --brief AFTER it fires — a
get run immediately after the external change may still show status None (rust2
#9). `minas read` does not trigger a reload (open document wins); only the
watcher / an Open on a changed file does.

name: exec
description: minas exec '<Command JSON>': raw command passthrough + the headless allowlist
body:
EXEC — raw command passthrough (advanced)

Use:      minas exec '<Command JSON>'        (examples: `"Save"`, `"GetState"`)
          minas exec '"Save"'                (the argument IS the JSON string)

What it does: sends one Command and prints the raw response. A snapshot response
prints the StateSnapshot JSON (same as before); lightweight responses (Hints /
Peek / ReviewComments / ServerInfo / Outline ...) print that response JSON
(rust2 #26).

Headless allowlist — anything else is rejected with status
"headless clients can only use ..." and minas exits 1:
    GetState, Save, WaitFor, DocumentEdit, Open, Close,
    ListReviewComments, ClearReviewComments,
    RegisterBaseRoot, UnregisterBaseRoot
- A rejected command is a NO-OP and exits 1 (rust2 #26). Do not treat the printed
  snapshot's status as success — check $?.
- TUI-only commands (Search, SetMode, Insert-mode keys, selection/view moves) are
  not on the allowlist. Use the dedicated subcommand instead: review, hover,
  outline, peek, hints, at, symbol, rename, references, check.
- RegisterBaseRoot / UnregisterBaseRoot have no dedicated subcommand — exec is
  the only way (ADR #53). They register a read-only comparison root.
- Prefer the dedicated subcommands in scripts; exec is for commands without one.
